claim: Cerebellar climbing fibers convey diverse signals.
source: Cerebellar climbing fibers convey diverse signals, but how they are organized in the compartmental structure of the cerebellar cortex during learning remains largely unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract introduction.

claim: Tensor component analysis revealed that a majority of climbing fiber inputs to Purkinje cells were reduced to only four functional components.
source: Tensor component analysis revealed that a majority of climbing fiber inputs to Purkinje cells were reduced to only four functional components, corresponding to accurate timing control of motor initiation related to a Go cue, cognitive error-based learning, reward processing, and inhibition of erroneous behaviors after a No-go cue.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the tensor component analysis performed on the experimental data.

evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the first tensor component (TC1) from the analysis.

claim: The second functional component corresponds to cognitive error-based learning.
source: Tensor component analysis revealed that a majority of climbing fiber inputs to Purkinje cells were reduced to only four functional components, corresponding to accurate timing control of motor initiation related to a Go cue, cognitive error-based learning, reward processing, and inhibition of erroneous behaviors after a No-go cue.

claim: The third functional component corresponds to reward processing.

claim: The fourth functional component corresponds to inhibition of erroneous behaviors after a No-go cue.

claim: Changes in neural activities during learning of the first two components were correlated with corresponding changes in timing control and error learning across animals.
source: Changes in neural activities during learning of the first two components were correlated with corresponding changes in timing control and error learning across animals, indirectly suggesting causal relationships.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data, acknowledged as indirect evidence.

evidence: This is based on analysis of synchrony changes across different conditions and learning stages.

claim: The cerebellum reduces dimensions of the learning space by dynamically organizing multiple functional components based on anatomical compartments.
source: These findings suggest that, in close collaborations with other brain regions including the inferior olive nucleus, the cerebellum, based on anatomical compartments, reduces dimensions of the learning space by dynamically organizing multiple functional components, a feature that may inspire new-generation AI designs.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of the findings, presented as a suggested mechanism.

claim: The cerebellum collaborates with other brain regions including the inferior olive nucleus in organizing functional components.
source: These findings suggest that, in close collaborations with other brain regions including the inferior olive nucleus, the cerebellum, based on anatomical compartments, reduces dimensions of the learning space by dynamically organizing multiple functional components, a feature that may inspire new-generation AI designs.

claim: Machine learning algorithms necessitate as many training data samples as the number of their parameters for correct generalization.
source: Computational learning theory asserts that machine learning algorithms necessitate as many training data samples as the number of their parameters for correct generalization (Watanabe, 2009; LeCun et al., 2015; Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Wurman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational learning theory literature.

claim: The cerebellum contains tens of billions of neurons and even more synapses.
source: In contrast, although the cerebellum contains tens of billions of neurons and even more synapses, and is involved in diverse functions (Strick et al., 2009; Sokolov et al., 2017), each of which may require a different coding scheme (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; De Zeeuw, 2021; De Zeeuw et al., 2021), animals can learn new behaviors within thousands of trials, for which the cerebellum is mainly responsible (Adolph et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the cerebellum.

claim: Cerebellar compartments and spike synchronization drastically reduce effective numbers of learning parameters.
source: To reconcile these observations, previous theories have proposed that cerebellar compartments (Andersson and Oscarsson, 1978; Ito, 1997; Nisimaru et al., 2013) and spike synchronization drastically reduce effective numbers of learning parameters (degrees of freedom) and enable learning from small samples (Kawato et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2017; Cortese et al., 2019; Kawato et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on previous theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cerebellar compartments and spike synchronization enable learning from small samples.
source: To reconcile these observations, previous theories have proposed that cerebellar compartments (Andersson and Oscarsson, 1978; Ito, 1997; Nisimaru et al., 2013) and spike synchronization drastically reduce effective numbers of learning parameters (degrees of freedom) and enable learning from small samples (Kawato et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2017; Cortese et al., 2019; Kawato et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on previous theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is organized into multiple longitudinal compartments with different intrinsic neuronal activity.
source: On one hand, the cerebellar cortex is organized into multiple longitudinal compartments with different intrinsic neuronal activity (Andersson and Oscarsson, 1978; Ito, 2013; Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Apps et al., 2018; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara et al., 2007; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Kano et al., 1990), each forming a computational unit (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each cerebellar compartment forms a computational unit.
source: On one hand, the cerebellar cortex is organized into multiple longitudinal compartments with different intrinsic neuronal activity (Andersson and Oscarsson, 1978; Ito, 2013; Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Apps et al., 2018; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara et al., 2007; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Kano et al., 1990), each forming a computational unit (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Aldolase C (AldC)-positive and negative zones represent distinct information in adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
source: Outstandingly in each of these, aldolase C (AldC)-positive and negative zones represent distinct information in adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (De Zeeuw and Koekkoek, 1997; Wylie et al., 1994; Schonewille et al., 2006) and in eyeblink conditioning (Hesslow, 1994a; Hesslow, 1994b; Mostofi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on vestibulo-ocular reflex.

claim: Aldolase C (AldC)-positive and negative zones represent distinct information in eyeblink conditioning.
source: Outstandingly in each of these, aldolase C (AldC)-positive and negative zones represent distinct information in adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (De Zeeuw and Koekkoek, 1997; Wylie et al., 1994; Schonewille et al., 2006) and in eyeblink conditioning (Hesslow, 1994a; Hesslow, 1994b; Mostofi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on eyeblink conditioning.

claim: Compartmentalization constitutes dimension reduction for cerebellar functions related to eye movement and conditioning.
source: Therefore, this compartmentalization constitutes, at least in part, dimension reduction for cerebellar functions related to eye movement and conditioning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on AldC zones and their functions.

claim: Synchronization of climbing fiber (CF) activity mainly originates from inferior olivary neurons.
source: On the other hand, synchronization of climbing fiber (CF) activity, which mainly originates from inferior olivary neurons (Llinas et al., 1974; Lang et al., 1999; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006), contributes strongly to cerebellar functions (Eccles et al., 1966; Nietz et al., 2017; Sedaghat-Nejad et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of CF activity, supported by citations.

claim: Synchronization of climbing fiber activity contributes strongly to cerebellar functions.
source: On the other hand, synchronization of climbing fiber (CF) activity, which mainly originates from inferior olivary neurons (Llinas et al., 1974; Lang et al., 1999; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006), contributes strongly to cerebellar functions (Eccles et al., 1966; Nietz et al., 2017; Sedaghat-Nejad et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CF synchronization and cerebellar function.

claim: CF synchrony might provide flexible dimension control of neural dynamics during acquisition of complex behaviors.
source: During acquisition of complex behaviors in motor activity (Welsh et al., 1995; Hoogland et al., 2015; Wagner et al., 2021) or reward processing (Wagner et al., 2017; Heffley and Hull, 2019; Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019), CF synchrony might provide flexible dimension control of neural dynamics (Kawato et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2017; Kawato et al., 2021; Hoang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Synchrony is high within cerebellar compartments, but not across them.
source: Moreover, synchrony is high within cerebellar compartments, but not across them, implying a structure-function relationship between cerebellar compartments and synchronization (Ozden et al., 2009; De Gruijl et al., 2014; Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies measuring synchrony within and across compartments.

claim: High synchrony within compartments but not across them implies a structure-function relationship between cerebellar compartments and synchronization.
source: Moreover, synchrony is high within cerebellar compartments, but not across them, implying a structure-function relationship between cerebellar compartments and synchronization (Ozden et al., 2009; De Gruijl et al., 2014; Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on compartmental synchrony.

claim: It is unclear how compartments and synchronization together facilitate dimension reduction for learning of cognitive functions.
source: However, it is unclear how compartments and synchronization together facilitate dimension reduction for learning of cognitive functions, for which genetic prewiring is unlikely to be sufficient.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Two-photon recordings of CF inputs to Purkinje cells were performed in eight AldC compartments of mice learning an auditory discrimination Go/No-go task.
source: To shed light on mechanisms of dimension reduction in the cerebellum, we systematically examined two-photon recordings of CF inputs to Purkinje cells in eight AldC compartments of mice learning an auditory discrimination Go/No-go task (Tsutsumi et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The auditory discrimination Go/No-go task requires reinforcement learning guided by reward.
source: This task requires reinforcement learning guided by reward, and necessitates, 1. accurate timing control of licking to obtain a reward, 2. learning based on reward prediction error, 3. reward processing, and 4. inhibition of licking to the No-go-cue.
evidence: This describes the task design and its requirements.

claim: The Go/No-go task necessitates accurate timing control of licking to obtain a reward.
source: This task requires reinforcement learning guided by reward, and necessitates, 1. accurate timing control of licking to obtain a reward, 2. learning based on reward prediction error, 3. reward processing, and 4. inhibition of licking to the No-go-cue.

source: We applied a hyper-acuity spike timing detection algorithm with 10 ms resolution (Hoang et al., 2020b) to estimate timing of complex spikes (CSs), which were reliably recorded by calcium imaging.
evidence: This describes the reliability of the recording method.

source: Tensor component analysis (Williams et al., 2018) of CS activity revealed that 50% of the variance was explained by only four clearly separable components (TC1-4), each corresponding to one of the above four functions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the tensor component analysis.

claim: Each of the four tensor components corresponds to one of the four task functions.
source: Tensor component analysis (Williams et al., 2018) of CS activity revealed that 50% of the variance was explained by only four clearly separable components (TC1-4), each corresponding to one of the above four functions.

source: Briefly, mice (n=17) were trained to associate the 'Go' cue (a 9 kHz tone for 0.5 s) with a licking during a response period of 1 s after cue onset to get a water reward.

evidence: This describes the experimental design for the No-go condition.

claim: 87 sessions were recorded from 17 mice, including 26,517 trials of auditory discrimination Go/No-go tasks in three learning stages.

claim: The lick rate remained relatively unchanged in HIT trials during learning.

claim: There was an increase in the fraction correct for the Go cue during learning (0.78±0.1 and 0.98±0.01, 1st and 6th sessions, respectively).

claim: There were no consistent changes in the reaction time after Go during learning.

evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral analysis.

claim: Lick-latency fluctuation decreased with learning (0.45±0.15 and 0.22±0.06, 1st and 6th sessions, respectively).

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figures 1C-D.

claim: For the No-go cue, the fraction incorrect decreased after learning (0.66±0.12 and 0.15±0.06, 1st and 6th sessions, respectively).

claim: The lick rate in the early response window (0–500ms after cue onset) for No-go cues decreased with learning (2.4±1.2 and 0.3±0.2 Hz, 1st and 6th sessions, respectively).

source: More strikingly, we found that a fraction of neurons represented multiple TCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the TC representation analysis.

claim: 'Green' neurons represented mixing of TC1-TC3 in AldC compartments 5a- and 5a+.
source: They were 'green' neurons for mixing of TC1-TC3 in AldC compartments 5a- and 5a+, and 'dark magenta' neurons for mixing of TC2-TC4 in the lateral Crus II at the first stage.
evidence: This is a specific example of neurons representing multiple TCs.

claim: 'Dark magenta' neurons represented mixing of TC2-TC4 in the lateral Crus II at the first stage.
source: They were 'green' neurons for mixing of TC1-TC3 in AldC compartments 5a- and 5a+, and 'dark magenta' neurons for mixing of TC2-TC4 in the lateral Crus II at the first stage.
evidence: This is a specific example of neurons representing multiple TCs.

claim: The tensor representation of individual neurons showed that TCs have complicated compartmental distributions that change during learning.
source: The tensor representation of individual neurons showed that TCs have complicated compartmental distributions that change during learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the visualization of TC representation.

claim: Single AldC compartments and single neurons can represent multiple TCs.
source: At the same time, single AldC compartments and single neurons can represent multiple TCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TC representation analysis.

claim: Fractions of TC1 and TC4 neurons increased significantly during learning.
source: We found that fractions of TC1 and TC4 neurons increased and those of TC2 and TC3 decreased significantly (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of TC neuron fractions across learning stages shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fractions of TC2 and TC3 neurons decreased significantly during learning.
source: We found that fractions of TC1 and TC4 neurons increased and those of TC2 and TC3 decreased significantly (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of TC neuron fractions across learning stages shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons in the lateral Crus II changed in opposite directions (p<0.0001 for changes in fractions across the three stages, n=150 sessions).
source: Interestingly, while fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons in the lateral Crus II (AldC compartments 7+to 5-) changed in opposite directions (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001 for changes in fractions across the three stages, n=150 sessions, Figure 6C), their summation remained unchanged at about 60% even at the session level (ANOVA and pairwise t-tests, p>0.3), suggesting that TC2 neurons were converted into TC4 neurons during learning.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of TC2 and TC4 neuron fractions shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The summation of TC2 and TC4 neuron fractions remained unchanged at about 60% even at the session level (p>0.3).
source: Interestingly, while fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons in the lateral Crus II (AldC compartments 7+to 5-) changed in opposite directions (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001 for changes in fractions across the three stages, n=150 sessions, Figure 6C), their summation remained unchanged at about 60% even at the session level (ANOVA and pairwise t-tests, p>0.3), suggesting that TC2 neurons were converted into TC4 neurons during learning.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TC2 neurons were converted into TC4 neurons during learning.
source: Interestingly, while fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons in the lateral Crus II (AldC compartments 7+to 5-) changed in opposite directions (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001 for changes in fractions across the three stages, n=150 sessions, Figure 6C), their summation remained unchanged at about 60% even at the session level (ANOVA and pairwise t-tests, p>0.3), suggesting that TC2 neurons were converted into TC4 neurons during learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that TC2 decreased while TC4 increased but their sum remained constant.

claim: The synchrony strength was significantly and negatively correlated with geographic distance (slope = –0.0004, p<0.0001).
source: We found that the synchrony strength was significantly and negatively correlated with both geographic distance (slope = –0.0004, p<0.0001, Figure 6D) and TC distance (slope = –0.07, p<0.0001, Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The synchrony strength was significantly and negatively correlated with TC distance (slope = –0.07, p<0.0001).
source: We found that the synchrony strength was significantly and negatively correlated with both geographic distance (slope = –0.0004, p<0.0001, Figure 6D) and TC distance (slope = –0.07, p<0.0001, Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Geographically close neurons tend to be more synchronized than distant ones.
source: These results suggest that geographically close neurons tend to be more synchronized than distant ones, and that neurons with similar TC coefficients tend to be more synchronized than those with different TC coefficients, even when canceling out the other factor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between synchrony and geographic distance.

claim: Neurons with similar TC coefficients tend to be more synchronized than those with different TC coefficients, even when canceling out the other factor.
source: These results suggest that geographically close neurons tend to be more synchronized than distant ones, and that neurons with similar TC coefficients tend to be more synchronized than those with different TC coefficients, even when canceling out the other factor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between synchrony and TC distance.

claim: Synchrony strength was higher for the within-compartment group (0.18±0.12) than for the across-compartment group (0.13±0.09, p<0.0001).
source: We found that synchrony strength was higher for the within-compartment group (mean ± std, 0.18±0.12) than for the across-compartment group (0.13±0.09, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001, Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison of within- and across-compartment synchrony shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both geographic distance and TC distance were lower for the within-compartment group than for the across-compartment counterpart (geographic distance, 43±31 and 114±53 μm; TC distance, 0.30±0.31 and 0.39±0.33 for within-compartment and across-compartment groups, respectively, p<0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons).
source: As expected, both geographic distance and TC distance were lower for the within-compartment group than for the across-compartment counterpart (geographic distance, 43±31 and 114±53 μm; TC distance, 0.30±0.31 and 0.39±0.33 for within-compartment and across-compartment groups, respectively, p<0.0001 for all pairwise comparisons using one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison of within- and across-compartment groups.

claim: All CS activity can be decomposed into only four components (TC1-4), which capture key features of behavior and learning.
source: First, we found that all CS activity can be decomposed into only four components (TC1-4), which capture key features of behavior and learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from tensor component analysis.

claim: This is a significant dimension reduction performed by the cerebellum.
source: This is a significant dimension reduction performed by the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that four components explain a large portion of variance.

claim: Compartmental representations of the four TC populations align well with functional and anatomical boundaries between medial and lateral parts of Crus II, as well as expression of Aldolase-C.
source: We also found that compartmental representations of these populations align well with functional and anatomical boundaries between medial and lateral parts of Crus II, as well as expression of Aldolase-C.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial distribution findings.

claim: CS synchrony, measured at single-trial level, was concentrated among neurons that belong to the same components.
source: Second, CS synchrony, measured at single-trial level, was concentrated among neurons that belong to the same components.
evidence: This is a summary of the synchrony analysis findings.

claim: The synchrony strength in different components may change in the opposite direction during learning.
source: Furthermore, the synchrony strength in different components may change in the opposite direction during learning, suggesting that CS synchrony is the neural mechanism that drives organization of those components.
evidence: This is a summary of the bidirectional synchrony changes observed.

claim: CS synchrony is the neural mechanism that drives organization of the tensor components.
source: Furthermore, the synchrony strength in different components may change in the opposite direction during learning, suggesting that CS synchrony is the neural mechanism that drives organization of those components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of synchrony changes during learning.

claim: Increase of CS synchrony in TC1 neurons may behaviorally decrease the lick fluctuation in Go trials across animals.
source: Third, we suggested that, increase of CS synchrony in TC1 neurons may behaviorally decrease the lick fluctuation in Go trials across animals.
evidence: This is a suggested relationship based on correlation analysis across animals.

claim: A decrease of the relative proportion of TC2 neurons may decrease cognitive error of No-go cues across animals.
source: In parallel for cognitive learning, a decrease of the relative proportion of TC2 neurons may decrease cognitive error of No-go cues across animals.
evidence: This is a suggested relationship based on correlation analysis across animals.

claim: The results indirectly imply causal relationships of TC1 with timing control and TC2 with cognitive error learning.
source: Together, these results indirectly imply causal relationships of TC1 with timing control and TC2 with cognitive error learning.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation of the correlation findings, acknowledging the indirect nature of the evidence.

claim: Bi-directional synchronous response-associated changes in CF activities, finely constructed on compartmental structure, could reduce the dimension of the learning space.
source: In summary, our study suggested that bi-directional synchronous response-associated changes in CF activities, finely constructed on compartmental structure, could reduce the dimension of the learning space and thus provide a flexible learning scheme in diverse cerebellar functions.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings into a proposed mechanism.

claim: Bi-directional synchronous response-associated changes in CF activities provide a flexible learning scheme in diverse cerebellar functions.
source: In summary, our study suggested that bi-directional synchronous response-associated changes in CF activities, finely constructed on compartmental structure, could reduce the dimension of the learning space and thus provide a flexible learning scheme in diverse cerebellar functions.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings into a proposed mechanism.

claim: The hyperacuity algorithm enabled study of a huge number of neurons (>6000) with hyperacuity resolution (10ms) along a whole process of cognitive and motor learning.
source: One of the valuable features of this study was that we applied the hyperacuity algorithm (Hoang et al., 2020b) to estimate CS timings from calcium responses with 10 ms resolution. This enabled us to study a huge number of neurons (>6000) with hyperacuity resolution (10ms) along a whole process of cognitive and motor learning, with precise spatial localization guided by boundaries between Aldolase-C (AldC) zones.
evidence: This describes the technical capability enabled by the hyperacuity algorithm.

claim: The first two tensor components are in good agreement with the dichotomy in the literature that CFs either function as 'error signals' or 'timing signals'.
source: Notably, the first two components are in good agreement with the dichotomy in the literature that CFs either function as "error signals" or "timing signals" (Mauk et al., 2000).
evidence: This relates the findings to existing theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: CFs projecting to TC1 neurons convey 'timing signals' to control early licks, in accordance with timing control hypothesis.
source: These results suggest that CFs projecting to TC1 neurons convey "timing signals" to control early licks, in accordance with timing control hypothesis (Lang et al., 1999; Welsh et al., 1995; Wagner et al., 2021; Llinás, 2013; Ohmae et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of TC1 function supported by citations to timing control literature.

claim: Increased CS synchrony could stabilize the timing of motor commands by canceling noisy synaptic inputs to the IO, or contributing to timed motor initiation by evoking rebound firing in downstream cerebellar nuclei.
source: That is, increased CS synchrony could stabilize the timing of motor commands by canceling noisy synaptic inputs to the IO, or contributing to timed motor initiation by evoking rebound firing in downstream cerebellar nuclei (Tsutsumi et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2019), possibly leading to more precise timing control with less fluctuation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis for how increased synchrony could affect timing control, supported by citations.

claim: TC2 neurons convey cognitive 'error signals' (unwarranted licks) specific to the No-go cue, in accordance with the Marr-Ito-Albus hypothesis.
source: These results suggested that TC2 neurons convey cognitive "error signals" (unwarranted licks) specific to the No-go cue, in accordance with the Marr-Ito-Albus hypothesis (Kawato et al., 2021; Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito, 1970).
evidence: This is an interpretation of TC2 function supported by citations to error signal literature.

claim: The results suggested causal relationships of TC1 with timing control and TC2 with cognitive learning.
source: Together with decoding analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and muscimol injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), all of those results suggested causal relationships of TC1 with timing control and TC2 with cognitive learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including correlations, decoding, and perturbation.

claim: The TC3 population showed only slight changes in CF firing and synchrony, except for becoming silent at the final learning stage for the FA condition.
source: In contrast to TC1 and TC2 populations that exhibited marked learning effects, the TC3 population showed only slight changes in CF firing and synchrony, except for becoming silent at the final learning stage for the FA condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the learning-related changes in TC3.

claim: The correlation between CSs of TC3 neurons with reward licks was high for HIT trials across all learning stages, suggesting the role of TC3 in reward processing.
source: The correlation between CSs of TC3 neurons with reward licks was high for HIT trials across all learning stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), suggesting the role of TC3 in reward processing.
evidence: This is an inference about TC3 function based on correlation with reward licks.

claim: TC4 is only related to CR trials.
source: We also found that TC4 is only related to CR trials (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the cue-response specificity of TC4 shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increased CS firing in TC4 neurons with learning, especially in AldC compartment 6+, led to the hypothesis that TC4 induces more successful suppression of early licks after the No-go cue.
source: Increased CS firing in TC4 neurons with learning, especially in AldC compartment 6+, led to the hypothesis that TC4 induces more successful suppression of early licks after the No-go cue, that is, an increase of CR trials and decrease of FA trials (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about TC4 function based on its learning-related changes.

claim: TC4 firings were correlated with suppression of licks following No-go cues compared to those in the pre-cue period.
source: Spike-triggered lick responses supported this idea; TC4 firings were correlated with suppression of licks following No-go cues compared to those in the pre-cue period (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is evidence supporting the hypothesis about TC4 function shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Populations of PC populations may optimize distinct sub-goals using their own neural mechanisms, but they may collectively serve a single task.
source: From a conceptual standpoint, the fact that motor, cognitive and reward elements are simultaneously represented by the four TCs suggest a new direction for future investigations of CF activity. That is, populations of PC populations may optimize distinct sub-goals using their own neural mechanisms, but they may collectively serve a single task.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the findings about multiple functional components.

claim: Learning in TC2 neurons is more important for the cognitive aspect of the present Go/No-go tasks, because the reward acquisition is determined by correct cue discrimination.
source: For instance, we insisted that learning in TC2 neurons is more important for the cognitive aspect of the present Go/No-go tasks, because the reward acquisition is determined by correct cue discrimination, while improved motor skills by learning in TC1 neurons would only maximize the reward amount per time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relative importance of different components for task performance.

claim: In eye-blink conditioning, timing control is more crucial than cue recognition because the conditioned response requires more temporal precision.
source: In eye-blink conditioning, which may contain similar cognitive and motor elements, timing control is more crucial than cue recognition because the conditioned response (e.g. closing the eyelid) requires more temporal precision.
evidence: This is a comparison to another task to illustrate how component importance may vary by task.

claim: Only four components seem to account for a wide variety of CF responses of Purkinje cells in eight AldC compartments.
source: From a computational learning-theory point of view, it is striking and extremely important that only four components seem to account for a wide variety of CF responses of Purkinje cells in eight AldC compartments.
evidence: This emphasizes the significance of the dimension reduction finding.

claim: Four TCs accounted for more than 50% of the variance of 6,445 neurons in four cue-response conditions, while about 20 TCs are needed to explain the same amount of variance for shuffled data.
source: We found that four TCs accounted for more than 50% of the variance of 6,445 neurons in four cue-response conditions, while about 20 TCs are needed to explain the same amount of variance for shuffled data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the permutation test shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Significant dimension reduction (fivefold) was demonstrated by the permutation test.
source: Consequently, significant dimension reduction (fivefold) was demonstrated by the permutation test.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the number of components needed for real vs. shuffled data.

claim: These four components also explain main learning effects in the Go/No-go experiment, that is, more precise timing control, error decrease, reward processing, and successful lick suppression.
source: It is worth noting that these four components also explain main learning effects in the Go/No-go experiment, that is, more precise timing control, error decrease, reward processing, and successful lick suppression.
evidence: This relates the four components to the main behavioral learning effects.

claim: Dimension reduction was further confirmed by conventional principal component analysis (PCA) showing d=67 dimensions explained 65% of variance.
source: Dimension reduction was further confirmed by conventional principal component analysis (PCA) showing d=67 dimensions (Mazzucato et al., 2016), significantly smaller than >6000 recorded neurons, explained 65% of variance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from PCA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dimension reduction by the cerebellum in Go/No-go tasks is remarkable compared to other brain regions in various tasks.
source: Such dimension reduction by the cerebellum in Go/No-go tasks is remarkable compared to other brain regions in various tasks, although dimension reduction may depend on complexity of the task (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the degree of dimension reduction, with citation to literature on other brain regions.

claim: If a learning system possesses many degrees of freedom, a huge training dataset is theoretically required.
source: Considering various factors involved in learning, such as auditory sensory inputs to the cerebellum representing different frequencies, relevant deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN), timing of licks with respect to auditory cues, and rewards, degrees of freedom of the Go/No-go tasks are huge. If a learning system possesses many degrees of freedom, a huge training dataset is theoretically required.
evidence: This is a statement from computational learning theory.

claim: Mice learned auditory discrimination Go/No-go task within hundreds of trials.
source: But mice learned auditory discrimination Go/No-go task within hundreds of trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data.

claim: The cerebellum reduces the degrees of freedom significantly, thanks to its zonal structure as well as effective mechanisms of dimension control by upstream networks such as gap-junctions in IO neurons.
source: This implies that the cerebellum reduces the degrees of freedom significantly, thanks to its zonal structure as well as effective mechanisms of dimension control by upstream networks such as gap-junctions in IO neurons (Hoang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanisms enabling dimension reduction, supported by citation.

claim: Dimensional reduction is beneficial for the whole brain during learning, by facilitating the coordination between the cerebellum, the cerebral cortex, and the basal ganglia in different learning stages.
source: Dimensional reduction is certainly beneficial for the whole brain during learning, by facilitating the coordination between the cerebellum, the cerebral cortex, and the basal ganglia in different learning stages (Bostan and Strick, 2018; Wagner and Luo, 2020; Kawato and Cortese, 2021; Kostadinov and Häusser, 2022; Wagner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of dimension reduction, supported by citations.

claim: CS synchrony was significantly stronger within TCs than across TCs.
source: We found that CS synchrony was significantly stronger within TCs than across TCs, and the highest synchrony was observed when TCs function in their dedicated cue-response conditions (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a result from the synchrony analysis shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: The highest synchrony was observed when TCs function in their dedicated cue-response conditions.
source: We found that CS synchrony was significantly stronger within TCs than across TCs, and the highest synchrony was observed when TCs function in their dedicated cue-response conditions (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a result from the synchrony analysis shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: CS synchrony was dependent on AldC expression and geographic distance.
source: While CS synchrony was dependent on AldC expression and geographic distance, as already reported (Hoogland et al., 2015; Tsutsumi et al., 2015), our analysis further showed that synchrony was stronger for pairs of neurons with smaller difference in their cue responsiveness, estimated by the TC distance (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is consistent with previous reports cited in the manuscript.

claim: Synchrony was stronger for pairs of neurons with smaller difference in their cue responsiveness, estimated by the TC distance.
source: While CS synchrony was dependent on AldC expression and geographic distance, as already reported (Hoogland et al., 2015; Tsutsumi et al., 2015), our analysis further showed that synchrony was stronger for pairs of neurons with smaller difference in their cue responsiveness, estimated by the TC distance (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is a new finding from the TC distance analysis shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: Synchronization, partially guided by anatomical structure, dynamically organizes diverse functions represented by TCs.
source: Together, these results suggested that synchronization, partially guided by anatomical structure, dynamically organizes diverse functions represented by TCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synchrony analyses.

claim: CS synchrony is spatially and temporally dynamic, in concert with the organization of TCs.
source: Remarkably, we also found that CS synchrony is spatially and temporally dynamic, in concert with the organization of TCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the dynamic synchrony findings.

claim: Synchronous firing decreased in TC2 neurons for the FA, but it increased in TC1 neurons for the HIT condition.
source: That is, synchronous firing decreased in TC2 neurons for the FA, but it increased in TC1 neurons for the HIT condition (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the opposite changes in synchrony shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Opposite changes in CS synchrony were strongly correlated with changes in cue responsiveness.
source: Such opposite changes in CS synchrony were strongly correlated with changes in cue responsiveness (Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Decoding analysis indicated that synchronous CSs better predict licking events than ordinary CSs.
source: Our decoding analysis indicated that synchronous CSs better predict licking events than ordinary CSs (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Highly synchronous CSs caused a large drop in DCN activity while isolated CSs produced only weak inhibition.
source: Furthermore, previous studies showed that highly synchronous CSs caused a large drop in DCN activity while isolated CSs produced only weak inhibition (Tang et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on DCN responses to synchronous CSs.

claim: Synchronous CS activity shapes DCN output generating motor commands.
source: These results together supported the view that synchronous CS activity shapes DCN output generating motor commands.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding analysis and cited literature.

claim: One mechanistic explanation for opposite changes in CS synchrony could be different synaptic plasticity rules between AldC-positive and -negative zones.
source: One mechanistic explanation could be different synaptic plasticity rules between AldC-positive and -negative zones. Note that TC1 is mainly distributed in AldC-positive zones (De Zeeuw, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation supported by citation.

claim: Enhanced CS synchrony in TC1 would induce synchronous activation of Purkinje cell ensembles, which in turn, would tune downstream systems to facilitate initiation and coordination of precise timing control of movement.
source: Enhanced CS synchrony in TC1 would induce synchronous activation of Purkinje cell ensembles, which in turn, would tune downstream systems to facilitate initiation and coordination of precise timing control of movement.
evidence: This is a functional hypothesis about the role of enhanced synchrony in TC1.

claim: Strong CS synchrony in TC2 neurons at the initial learning stage would reduce the dimensionality of high-dimensional cognitive error signals for fast learning.
source: In contrast, strong CS synchrony in TC2 neurons at the initial learning stage would reduce the dimensionality of high-dimensional cognitive error signals for fast learning.
evidence: This is a functional hypothesis about the role of high synchrony in TC2 at early learning stages.

claim: At later stages, low CS synchrony would increase the dimensionality of cerebellar output for fine and sophisticated learning.
source: At later stages, low CS synchrony would increase the dimensionality of cerebellar output for fine and sophisticated learning (Kawato et al., 2011; Tokuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a functional hypothesis about the role of low synchrony at later learning stages, supported by citations.

claim: Dimensions of CS firings in TC1 and TC2 neurons decreased and increased, respectively, in accordance with changes in their CS synchrony.
source: This argument was supported by the result showing that dimensions of CS firings in TC1 and TC2 neurons decreased and increased, respectively, in accordance with changes in their CS synchrony (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a result from dimensionality analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Opposite changes in the dimension could be realized by interaction between electrical synapses in the IO and positive feedback loop of PC, DCN, and IO.
source: These opposite changes in the dimension could be realized by interaction between electrical synapses in the IO and positive feedback loop of PC, DCN, and IO, but future experiments are needed to test these possibilities.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation that requires future testing.

claim: Synchronized CSs of TC2 neurons may also convey motor commands to control early licks in No-go trials.
source: Beside their correlation with error signals, synchronized CSs of TC2 neurons may also convey motor commands to control early licks in No-go trials (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the spike-triggered lick response analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A mixed representation of error information and motor-related variables in CSs was observed in hand movement and saccade.
source: Such a duality of motor control and cognitive learning has never been reported, despite a mixed representation of error information and motor-related variables, for example direction of movement, in CSs was observed in hand movement (Kitazawa et al., 1998; Sendhilnathan et al., 2021; Ikezoe et al., 2023) and saccade (Markanday et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mixed representations in other motor tasks.

claim: Synchronized CSs of TC2 neurons contribute to generation of motor commands in downstream systems to inhibit the licking following No-go cues.
source: This finding implies that synchronized CSs of TC2 neurons do not simply multiplex complementary behavioral information. Rather, they contribute to generation of motor commands in downstream systems to inhibit the licking following No-go cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dual role of TC2 neurons.

claim: PCs involved in cognitive learning are assumed to modulate simple spikes (SSs) that also induce licks in FA trials.
source: One possible interpretation is that PCs, which are involved in cognitive learning, are assumed to modulate simple spikes (SSs) that also induce licks in FA trials.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) may occur by co-activation of parallel fibers and CF inputs to PCs involved in cognitive learning.
source: Long-term depression (LTD) may occur by co-activation of parallel fibers and CF inputs to these PCs (Ito and Kano, 1982; Wang et al., 2000; Doi et al., 2005; Jörntell and Hansel, 2006).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to LTD literature.

claim: As a result of LTD, simple spikes (SSs) tend to be modulated so that fewer erroneous licks are generated.
source: As a result, simple spikes (SSs) tend to be modulated so that fewer erroneous licks are generated.
evidence: This is a predicted consequence of the LTD mechanism.

claim: In eye-blink conditioning, SS suppression is correlated with conditioned blink responses on a trial-by-trial basis in awake mice.
source: We note that suppression of SSs may drive the movement in other learning schemes. For instance, in eye-blink conditioning, SS suppression is correlated with conditioned blink responses on a trial-by-trial basis in awake mice (ten Brinke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on eye-blink conditioning.

claim: TC2 and TC4 neurons possess almost identical temporal response profiles and overlapping spatial distributions.
source: It is interesting that TC2 and TC4 neurons (both responded actively to the No-go cue) possess not only almost identical temporal response profiles and overlapping spatial distributions (Figure 3), but also the largest overlap among TCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the TC analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TC2 and TC4 neurons have the largest overlap among TCs.
source: It is interesting that TC2 and TC4 neurons (both responded actively to the No-go cue) possess not only almost identical temporal response profiles and overlapping spatial distributions (Figure 3), but also the largest overlap among TCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons decreased and increased significantly, but summation of their fractions remained unchanged during the course of learning.
source: Furthermore, although fractions of TC2 and TC4 neurons decreased and increased significantly, summation of their fractions remained unchanged during the course of learning (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from the fraction analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TC2 and TC4 neurons are of the same neuron population, but they changed their cue-response specificity (FA to CR) due to LTD of parallel-fiber-Purkinje-cell synapses guided by CF inputs.
source: We hypothesized that TC2 and TC4 neurons are of the same neuron population, but that they changed their cue-response specificity (FA to CR) due to LTD of parallel-fiber-Purkinje-cell synapses guided by CF inputs (Yamamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between TC2 and TC4, supported by citation to LTD literature.

claim: Future simultaneous recordings of SSs and CSs as well as downstream systems may reveal neural mechanisms of TC2 and TC4 neurons.
source: Future simultaneous recordings of SSs and CSs as well as downstream systems may reveal neural mechanisms of TC2 and TC4 neurons.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.

claim: Activities of the four TC populations were of neurons sampled in different recording sessions.
source: Limitations of the current study are that activities of the four TC populations described above were of neurons sampled in different recording sessions, and that we did not investigate in detail single populations throughout learning.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study did not investigate in detail single populations throughout learning.
source: Limitations of the current study are that activities of the four TC populations described above were of neurons sampled in different recording sessions, and that we did not investigate in detail single populations throughout learning.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study design.

claim: Monitoring population activities as learning proceeds, combined with causal analysis of neuronal responses and behavior changes, is needed to understand diverse CF functions across TC populations.
source: Thus, monitoring population activities as learning proceeds, combined with causal analysis of neuronal responses and behavior changes, is needed to understand diverse CF functions across TC populations.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research to address the study's limitations.

claim: CFs may multiplex motor, cognitive and reward-related information.
